parts:
Hi all,
i have been trying to investigate why running my PCA-analysis in MSiReader gives me vastly different results to what I get in Cardinal, and I noticed that MSiReader found a lot more peaks. This was caused by the fact that when reading in my data to Cardinal with default parameters, they were binned to only about 3000 bins points, resulting in less than 500 detected peaks. Trying to imrove that, i am now reading in my data with higher resolution (I tried resolution = 0.004 and 0.0005 m/z), and not surprisingly, peakPick finds a lot more peaks, about 75000 (600000 for higher res). However, peakAlign now fails to align them, even though the mean spectrum (which as far as I understand is used to find the reference peaks) looks reasonable. I tried various different values for tolerance and max.diff, but the output data is always just a matrix of 0 (with about 13000 m/z values). Does anybody have some advice on what is the best resolution for reading in the data (in the manual it does say the machine's resolution, which I presume is the sampling rate, in order not to lose too many datapoints) and on what else I could test to figure out where the problem lies? I pasted my code below,
thanks so much,
ilona

data <- readMSIData(rawdata_filename, resolution=0.0005, units="mz", attach.only=TRUE)

dataP1 <- Cardinal::normalize(data, method="tic")

dataP2 <- Cardinal::peakPick(dataP1, method="simple", SNR=3)

plot(dataP2, pixel=1:ncol(dataP2), main = paste("Mean Spectrum"))

dataP3 <- Cardinal::peakAlign(dataP2, method="diff", tolerance=2.5, units="ppm")

messages.author: 6033d3c0e7d242fa
messages.subject: Re: Peak align fails
parts:
A few things I'll note first:

- The most recent versions of software are R 3.6, Bioconductor 3.9, and Cardinal 2.2
- You're using R 3.5, Bioconductor 3.8, and Cardinal 2.0
- Cardinal 2.2 is a big update, so you may want update when you're able

Apparently peakPick() and peakAlign() for MSImageSet are still using the older Hashmat class to store the peaks; this is a problem here because the m/z values end up being rounded to create the feature names that identify the peaks.

This isn't an issue for the newer MSImagingExperiment class, which uses the actual m/z values to identify the peaks. You can coerce the dataset to an MSImagingExperiment object with as(), or read it in that way when importing:

# read as MSImagingExperiment
myData <- readMSIData("path/to/file.imzML", as="MSImagingExperiment")

# OR coerce to MSImagingExperiment
myDataNew <- as(myDataOld, "MSImagingExperiment")

This class behaves similarly to the old MSImageSet class in most cases, but with better support for higher resolution experiments and some other new features.

The default in Cardinal 2.2 is to use MSImagingExperiment rather than MSImageSet.

Hopefully this would fix the issue.

Also note that the "tolerance" argument is actually for peakAlign() when used on "MSImagingExperiment", so it wasn't being used before (it expects 'diff.max" when used on an "MSImageSet"). This was another part of the problem. Sorry for the confusion during this transition from MSImageSet to MSImagingExperiment workflows...

-Kylie

messages.author: 6033d3c0e7d242fa
messages.subject: Re: Peak align fails
parts:
The code that I posted plots the spectrum that is being processed, with the pre-processing steps applied. The process() function takes a "plot" parameter that will plot the processing performed on each spectrum (if possible). (This is significantly slower than not plotting them, so should be used primarily to identify appropriate processing parameters for a few representative spectra.)

The good news: I was able to reproduce your issue myself and figure out the issue.

A bit of background: peakPick() using method="simple" and method="adaptive" work by dividing the spectrum into some number of regions, calculating the kurtosis (a statistical measure of "peakedness") on each region, and then tries to use the standard deviation of the relatively "flat" portions of the spectrum to estimate the noise.

The problem: The noise was being estimated as NaN, because there were no "flat" portions of the spectrum to use to estimate the noise.

The reason: When binning at a finer resolution, there will be some portions of the spectrum that are "empty", where no data was recorded (because nothing was detected). However, there will typically be a few blips where an intensity was recorded anyway, even if it that intensity is close to 0 (relative to the other intensities). This causes a very "spiky" spectrum in regions that should be flat, where intensities are either 0 or some minimal non-zero intensity. This results in no regions of the spectrum being used to calculate the noise, and the noise is calculated as NaN. This means the SNR's are also calculated as NaN, so no peaks are detected.

The solution: The method is actually working as intended, but there are a few solutions to the underlying issue--

1. Use peakPick(method="mad"). This is the simplest, immediate solution, and should hopefully result in plenty of detected peaks. This tells the algorithm you are mad at it and it must return you usable results, or else. (Joking.) This is a new method in 2.2 that uses the mean-absolute-deviation of successive differences in intensities, and does not rely on detecting "flat" portions of the spectrum, so it should avoid the above issue.

2. Remove the "empty" regions of the spectrum with mzFilter(). This is a new pre-processing method added in 2.2 that (by default) removes mass features with mean intensities below some proportion of the maximum mean intensity. Depending on your chosen bin resolution and how the machine collected the data, it's possible that this will actually leave you with only peaks on its own, and peak detection may not be necessary.

3. Try providing a "blocks=" argument to peakPick(method="simple") with a value larger than 100 (the default). By breaking the spectrum into more regions, the algorithm may find a flat-enough portion to estimate the noise better. I don't recommend this approach, as the noise will likely be under-estimated from regions that almost entirely 0 intensity, but it should work for a sufficiently large value of "blocks".

What I will do: Because the method is technically working as intended, there is nothing for me to "fix". However, keeping a default that may result in no detected peaks for "processed" imzML in a difficult-to-diagnose way is a problem. 

In the current release: I will patch the current release to issue a warning and a suggestion to use method="mad" if there are no appropriate regions of the spectrum to accurately estimate the noise using method="simple" and method="adaptive". I will try to do this tomorrow, although it may take a few days after that for the Bioconductor servers to see the update.

In the next release: I will change the default peak-picking method to "mad". I don't want to do this in the middle of a release cycle, but it seems like an appropriate thing to do for the next release if the method is more resilient to issues like this. IME, this method is sometimes too sensitive and has a tendency to estimate noise = 0 in cases like this, but I suppose that's far less of a problem than not detecting peaks at all. Edit: I will also try tweaking method="mad" to have better specificity...

Hopefully the above suggestions will be enough to fix your peak detection issue, and hopefully the peak alignment issue was indeed due to MSImageSet's datedness and hopefully using MSImagingExperiment will fix that once you have peaks.

Thank you for your help isolating this issue (which happens to be completely unrelated to your original issue!) as well as pointing out the typo in the vignette. I will fix that as well.

Let me know if you continue to have issues.

-Kylie

messages.author: 6033d3c0e7d242fa
messages.subject: Re: Peak align fails
parts:
I am not sure how to interpret the m/z values appearing rounded, as there should be no rounding if you're working with MSImagingExperiment. R may print fewer significant digits for some numbers than others, which may look like rounding. The bins start at the next-lowest-integer relative to the first observed m/z-value in the dataset, so the first few m/z-values may appear "neater" than the last, after many many small numbers have been accumulated. This is likely just an issue with the number of decimal places R chooses to print.

It is difficult to determine the best pre-processing parameters for data unseen or in a general case, which is why they are available for the user to adjust.

However, you're correct that if you want to distinguish peaks with an accuracy of m/z 0.002, then the data should be binned with a much higher resolution than 0.002; otherwise, you're not getting any peak shape, which is typically necessary for the peak picking to work properly. Attempting align peaks with the same tolerance as was originally used to bin the data doesn't really accomplish anything that couldn't be accomplished more simply by filtering the mass features, which may be what you should be doing instead.

The "holes" you're seeing are likely indeed spectra where that peak was not detected. This is typically going to happen when peak-picking on individual spectra and aligning the peaks. That's the purpose of peakBin(): to sweep back through the dataset and bin peaks using a list of reference m/z values. However, for peak binning to work also requires the peak shape, because the algorithm attempts to look for the peak center and then expand it to the local minima. If you're expecting the find peaks 0.002 m/z apart but you're data is already binned to 0.002 m/z resolution, then this will likely not work out, which may also be the source of your "holes". In this situation, you may need to use mzBin() with the reference m/z's of the peaks; mzBin() does not use the peak shape, and instead just bins to some fixed bin width.

If you want to extract peaks that are 0.002 apart but your data is already binned to 0.002, then you may try using mzFilter() with thresh.max=0.01 or something like that. This will just calculate the mean spectrum and then remove any m/z values with intensities less than some threshold proportion of the maximum mean intensity. This may produce the kind of dataset you want. (After doing this, you may want to set centroided(data) <- TRUE.)

I would suggest either:

1. Using either a higher bin resolution or a larger tolerance to do peak picking + binning.
2. If using .002 resolution, try using mzBin with the reference m/z's of the peaks instead of peakBin.
3. If using .002 resolution, try using mzFilter and skipping formal peak picking entirely

Hopefully one of these approaches may work for you.
